name: Redis
workload: memtier-style GET and SET throughput, pipeline 1 and pipeline 30, 40-shard Redis 7.0 Cluster versus a single Dragonfly process on an AWS c6gn.16xlarge (64 vCPU), as described in a Redis blog post on Redis architecture versus Dragonfly.
claimed_speedup: Redis cluster 18% to 40% greater throughput than Dragonfly while using only 40 of 64 vCores; pipelined GET 22.9M ops/sec versus Dragonfly 15.9M (derived ratio 1.44x); pipelined SET 19.85M versus 14M (derived ratio 1.42x) (snippet only, see caveats)
license: BSD-3-Clause (7.2.x and earlier); RSAL-2.0 or SSPL-1.0 (7.4 to 7.8); RSAL-2.0, SSPL-1.0 or AGPL-3.0 tri-license (8.0 and later)
tradeoffs: The win needs a 40-process Redis Cluster (key sharding, no cross-slot multi-key operations, cluster management) while Dragonfly serves the same machine from one multi-threaded process. A single Redis process stays single-threaded for command execution (I/O threads aside). Licence changed in 7.4 and 8.0; the benchmarked 7.0 line is BSD-3-Clause.
caveats: Weak record, kept because no other Redis-faster claim was reachable. (1) Snippet only: redis.io, redis.com and the mailing mirrors are EGRESS_BLOCKED (getaddrinfo ENOTFOUND), so the Redis blog post was never opened; the numbers come from two WebSearch result summaries of the post and benchmark_url is null for that reason. Re-check against the post before trusting any number. (2) Vendor-run: Redis Ltd wrote it as a rebuttal to Dragonfly's own claim of 25x over a single Redis process (dragonflydb.io blog, not opened); Dragonfly reproduced numbers were run by Redis. (3) Dragonfly's own repo benchmark on m5.large shows near parity (Redis 159K SET and 194K GET QPS versus Dragonfly 173K and 191K, from search snippet). (4) Independent Redis versus memcached write-ups (DZone m5.2xlarge, about 1.2M ops/sec memcached versus 1.0M Redis 7; oneuptime 2026 blog) show memcached ahead, and a Momento test (Valkey 8.1.1 about 999.8K SET/s versus Redis 8.0 729.4K) shows Valkey ahead. (5) No numeric Redis-versus-SQLite or Redis-versus-BerkeleyDB comparison exists in the README (no benchmark text), repo release notes or docs reachable here; Redis 8 headline gains (87% faster commands, 2x throughput) compare against Redis 7.4, not another system. Flags, compiler and exact memtier command unknown.

name: Reindexer
baseline: SQLite 3.17.0 (mattn/go-sqlite3, in-memory shared cache with indexes); also compared with Redis, Tarantool, MySQL, MongoDB, Elasticsearch, Sphinx, ArangoDB, RethinkDB
workload: 100K-document set (id, name, year with tree index, description with text index); Go benchmarks in-process on one core for get-by-id, 1-condition and 2-condition queries (limit 10) and full-text; plus wrk web benchmark on 8 cores for by-id, filters, full-text and update.
claimed_speedup: Single core get by ID 4,224 ns/op versus SQLite 23,735 (5.6x, derived from page data) and Redis 47,492 (11.2x, derived from page data); 1 condition 17,403 versus SQLite 60,749 (3.5x derived) and Redis 126,484 (7.3x derived); full-text exact 39,722 versus SQLite 1,274,902 (32x derived). Web, 8 cores, embedded mode: by ID 158,797 RPS versus SQLite 28,496 (5.6x derived) and Redis 79,411 (2.0x derived); 1 filter 70,149 versus SQLite 21,796 (3.2x derived); update 27,000 versus SQLite 452.
compiler_and_flags: Go 1.9.3 and clang-802.0.42 (Apple clang); optimisation flags not stated
hardware: 2.7 GHz Intel Core i7, MacBook Pro Retina 15-inch mid 2016 (exact SKU not stated); web runs in Ubuntu 16.04 Docker on the same laptop with 8 cores
tradeoffs: In-memory database: the whole data set lives in RAM (persisted to disk, but sized by memory). C++ core with a Go API; other bindings and a standalone server mode exist (standalone mode is 30 to 35 percent slower than embedded in the web table). Document model with its own query builder, not a plain key-value API.
caveats: First-party benchmark (Restream) on one 2016 laptop with 2018-era versions (Go 1.9.3, Tarantool 1.7.6.12, Elasticsearch 5.4.3, SQLite 3.17.0, MongoDB 3.4.5); optimisation flags and exact CPU SKU not stated, so tier C rather than A. The README labels Redis '2.3.9', which looks like a client or typo rather than a server release; Redis is reached over TCP on 127.0.0.1:6379 through go-redis while Reindexer and SQLite run in-process, so the Redis and other server rows include a network round trip (reindexer-benchmarks repo/redis.go). Redis 1-condition query is a ZRANGEBYSCORE on a sorted set of JSON blobs and Redis has no 2-condition or full-text row. Reindexer is NOT fastest on update in the web table: Redis 30,025 RPS and Tarantool 33,905 RPS beat embedded Reindexer 27,000. 'Object cache' rows (2,530 ns/op) skip unmarshalling in the other databases, so are not like for like. The benchmark repo imports an internal module path (git.restream.ru/itv-backend/reindexer) instead of the public GitHub path. Reindexer main README claims only 'on par with a typical key-value database' and up to 500K by-id queries/sec per core. Initial category guess was caches; moved to embedded-kv because the benchmark's closest like-for-like baseline is in-process SQLite.

name: Sophia
workload: Random reads on the Sophia author's SSD-based machine, per the sphia.org benchmark page as quoted in a September 2013 bitcoin-development mailing list post; Sophia v1.x era.
claimed_speedup: 438,084 random reads/sec for Sophia versus 167,476 random reads/sec for LevelDB (2.6x, derived from the quoted figures); against HyperLevelDB the gap is much smaller and HyperLevelDB writes randomly faster than Sophia (snippet only, see caveats)
stars_or_usage: 1.9k stars; storage engines of Amelia and Monotone are 'heavily inspired' by it (per README)
tradeoffs: MVCC, append-only, ACID, RAM-disk hybrid engine in plain C with zero dependencies, amalgamated source; O(1) worst-case read, write and range scan is the stated design target. Key-value plus row/document API, not SQL. Author states the project is no longer developed.
caveats: Snippet only: sphia.org, sophia.systems and the mailing-list mirrors (lists.linuxfoundation.org, gnusha.org, mirror.b10c.me) are EGRESS_BLOCKED (getaddrinfo ENOTFOUND), so neither the benchmark page nor the post was opened; the two figures come from WebSearch result summaries quoting the 2013 post, which says the poster had not reproduced the numbers. benchmark_url is null for that reason. Benchmark code, compiler, flags, CPU, key and value sizes and LevelDB version unknown; numbers predate Sophia 1.2 and the current 2.x line, and LevelDB has changed since. The repo README and docs index (SUMMARY.md) contain no benchmark results, only Big-O claims. Last commit 2026-03-03 is a README edit; the README says the project is no longer developed, so maintenance is recorded as abandoned. No SQLite or BerkeleyDB comparison found.
